common_name: Fresh Look Gold Celosia (AAS-Winning Compact Golden Plumed Celosia)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost at warm soil temperature and set out transplants once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Fresh Look Gold is a compact plumed selection bred to hold its bright golden color without browning through the full summer season.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all danger of frost has passed, spacing plants to allow good air movement around the dense plumes. Fresh Look Gold produces large, upright, feathery golden-yellow plumes on a tidy, uniform, well-branched plant that stays proportional rather than leggy, making it dependable for the front to middle of a mixed summer border or a patio container. Unlike older gold celosia strains that dulled or browned as the season progressed, this selection was specifically bred to hold a clean, bright gold color from first bloom through fall frost. Light monthly feeding and even moisture during establishment encourage the largest plumes, and cutting a few stems for fresh or dried arrangements only stimulates further branching.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Fresh Look Orange Celosia (Compact Marmalade-Orange Plumed Celosia)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil and night temperatures are consistently warm; Fresh Look Orange is a companion color to the Fresh Look series bred for the same compact habit and fade-resistant plumes.

directions: Set out transplants after the last frost into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and avoid overly rich soil that pushes soft growth at the expense of flowering. Fresh Look Orange carries dense, plume-shaped flower heads in a warm marmalade orange that reads well from a distance and pairs naturally with blue salvias, purple angelonia, or bronze foliage companions in a mixed summer bed. The compact 12-18 inch habit stays uniform without staking and performs reliably in both ground beds and large containers through peak Gulf Coast heat. Harvest stems for fresh arrangements as the plumes fully color, or hang them to dry for long-lasting winter bouquets, since the color holds well after drying.

common_name: Kelos Candela Pink Celosia (Compact Candle-Spike Wheat Celosia)
scientific_name: Celosia argentea var. spicata 'Kelos Candela Pink'

planting.note: Start indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost; Kelos Candela Pink is a compact, free-branching spicata (wheat-type) celosia bred for uniform bedding and container performance rather than tall cut-stem production.

directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun once the weather is reliably warm, and avoid soggy or poorly drained sites where the crown can rot in humid weather. Kelos Candela Pink produces dense clusters of slender, candle-like flower spikes in a soft rose-pink that stand well above tidy, compact foliage, giving a fuller, more branched silhouette than older wheat-type celosias grown mainly for cutting. Its bred-in weather tolerance keeps the plant blooming through heavy summer rain and humidity that can cause taller spicata types to flop. Light, regular feeding through the season keeps the branching spikes coming, and spent stems can simply be left in place since deadheading is not required for continued bloom.
sources: Benary — Celosia Kelos series breeding documentation

common_name: Cramer's Burgundy Celosia (Giant Deep Burgundy Crested Cockscomb)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger passes; this tall heirloom cockscomb selection needs the full length of a warm season to develop its large, velvety crests.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake or grow among sturdy neighbors, since the heavy, wide crests can become top-heavy on the tall stems as they mature. Cramer's Burgundy is a well-branched heirloom cockscomb selection, typically producing fifteen to twenty stems per plant, each topped with a velvety, deeply fluted crest in a rich wine-burgundy that darkens further as the season progresses and the weather cools. It was originally selected by a commercial cut-flower grower for reliable branching and drying quality, and it remains a favorite for fresh cutting and for air-drying, since the dense, corrugated crest retains its color and form for months once fully cured. Consistent moisture and full sun through crest formation produce the largest, most richly colored heads; cut for drying once the crest has fully expanded and firmed.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Cut Flower Trials

common_name: Bombay Purple Celosia (Uniform Cut-Flower Crested Cockscomb)

planting.note: Start indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into full sun; unlike many celosia, Bombay series plants should not be pinched, since pinching delays and reduces crest formation in this line.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and skip the usual pinching step used for bushier bedding celosia, since Bombay Purple is bred to send its energy into one large, uniform crest per stem rather than multiple side branches. The wide, ribbon-folded crest opens in a deep violet-purple that is darker on the outer folds and paler toward the center, reaching well over a foot across on a single sturdy stem, which is what makes this selection so valued for cut-flower and dried-flower production. Even, consistent moisture and full sun through the several weeks of crest expansion give the largest, most uniform heads, and the short, predictable time to harvest suits succession planting for cut-flower growers. Cut stems hold well in fresh arrangements and dry readily for long-lasting everlasting bouquets.

common_name: Sparkler Mix Celosia (Compact Multicolor Plumed Celosia Series)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once weather is reliably warm; Sparkler is a shorter-stemmed plumed celosia mix, best suited to bedding and container use rather than long cut stems.

directions: Transplant into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, spacing plants closely enough to form a solid mass of color in beds or mixed containers. Sparkler produces short, feathery flame-shaped plumes in a mix of red, gold, and cream-yellow tones on compact, well-branched plants, giving a fuller, more floriferous look than taller plumed strains grown primarily for cutting. The shorter stems make it a better fit for edging, mass bedding, and container combinations than for the cutting garden, where the paler cream and yellow tones in the mix tend to be the weaker growers. Light, even watering and a monthly feeding keep plants blooming steadily from early summer through the first fall frost.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Cut Flower Trials

common_name: Sylphid Celosia (Tall Lime-Green Plumed Cutting Celosia)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun after frost danger passes; Sylphid is a tall, upright plumed celosia grown mainly for its unusual color, so give it room and support among sturdy bed-mates.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving plants enough spacing for good airflow around the tall, upright plumes. Sylphid is a distinctive cutting celosia grown for its long, silky, feathery plumes that open in a soft lime green and gradually shift toward a warm creamy yellow as they age, a two-tone effect that is unusual among plumed celosia and pairs beautifully with both cool and hot color schemes in mixed arrangements. Because plants grow tall and top-heavy with flower, light staking or growing among dense neighbors helps keep stems upright through summer storms. Harvest stems as the plumes reach full size for fresh cutting, or hang them to dry for arrangements that keep their soft green-to-gold coloring for months.
